title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
text:
November 25, 2026
Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
- Federal Reserve Board
For release at 3:00 p.m. EST
The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing).
By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations.
Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.

title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans
text:
November 25, 2026
Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
- Federal Reserve Board
- Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
For release at 3:00 p.m. EST
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500.
The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026.
The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases.

title: Bowman, Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
text:
November 25, 2026
Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman
At the ASBA–BCBS–FSI High-Level Meeting for the Americas on Banking Supervision, Brasília, Brazil (via pre-recorded video)
Good morning.1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective.
First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized.
Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS.
Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort.
These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both.
Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action
One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly.
The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure.
The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure.2
Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them.
A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?
text:
The size of global corporate bond markets has increased dramatically over the past three decades. As of the end of 2024, nonfinancial corporate bonds issued by U.S. firms accounted for 29 percent of U.S. GDP. In other advanced economies, though bond markets remain smaller than in the U.S., corporate bonds were on average 11 percent of GDP in the same year. This growth is usually read as a shift from bank to market finance. But the ratio of bonds to GDP can rise either because firms take more debt in general, or because firms shift the composition of their debt toward bonds. In this post, we document growth in bonds to GDP for both the U.S. and other advanced economies, and argue that the sources of that growth are different across countries and have changed over time.
Why does the distinction between sources of growth matter? If bond markets grow because firms substitute away from banks, conditions in the bond market govern a larger share of corporate liabilities and bank lending standards a smaller one. That matters because, as we discussed in a prior Liberty Street Economics post, credit conditions in the two markets can be disconnected. If instead bond markets grow because firms borrow more of everything, the balance between the two is unchanged and firms are simply more exposed to both.
How Much Have Corporate Bond Markets Grown?
We start by documenting the overall trends in the size of the corporate bond markets around the world relative to the size of the economy. The chart below plots the time series of nonfinancial debt securities outstanding (that is, corporate bonds issued by nonfinancial firms resident in a country) as a percentage of GDP, for the U.S. and an equal-weighted average of other advanced economies.
Global Corporate Bonds Markets Were Growing Steadily Before the COVID-19 Pandemic
Starting with the U.S., we see that the corporate bond market grew from 12.2 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 36.2 percent in 2020, nearly a tripling in market size over seventy years. Turning to the other advanced economies, the growth rate of market size has been even faster, with bonds as a percentage of GDP more than doubling over a span of only twenty-four years for the average country, from 5.0 percent in 1996 to 12.2 percent in 2020. While the size of global bond markets is particularly large in 2020 because of COVID-19-pandemic-era issuance, the chart shows that bond markets were growing steadily in the preceding decades. In contrast, relative to GDP, bond market size retreated between 2021 and 2024, mostly driven by outsized GDP growth.
The chart also shows that U.S. corporate bond markets remain large relative to those of other advanced economies. This reflects structural differences between the U.S. financial system, which relies heavily on market-based finance, and the bank-centric financial systems in other advanced economies, notably European countries. In the rest of this post, we decompose the growth in bond market size into the change in bonds outstanding as a percentage of total nonfinancial corporate debt (that is, the composition of corporate debt) and the change in total corporate debt relative to GDP (a measure of how much nonfinancial firms borrow relative to the size of the economy; as a shorthand we will refer to growth in this measure as “credit deepening”).
Before the Pandemic, Credit Deepening Drove Growth in the United States, but Not Elsewhere
The next chart focuses on understanding the pre-pandemic trend in corporate bond market growth at the country level. Starting with the U.S. (left-most bar), we see that most of the growth in the size of the corporate bond market in the U.S. between 1996 and 2019 was due to credit deepening. That is, while the U.S. bond market grew by 9.2 percent of GDP over that twenty-three-year period, total credit to U.S. nonfinancial corporations grew from 41 percent of GDP to 52 percent, accounting for 6.6 percentage points of that growth; the bond share of corporate de

title: What Do Foreign Trends Tell Us About Future U.S. Labor Force Dynamics?
text:
Growth in the U.S. working-age population has fallen to near zero with the recent sharp drop in net immigration. Given the ongoing decline in the native-born working-age population, the available labor supply could soon begin to shrink. The demographic path the U.S. may soon navigate has already been trod by several other advanced economies that have experienced more rapid population aging and historically lower immigration. This post lays out the basic facts about advanced economy (AE) experiences since 2014 and raises the prospect that the demographic headwinds long visible abroad may now be coming into clear view at home.
Demographic and Labor Force Trends
The table below shows percentage changes in three variables from 2014 to 2025: working-age (ages 15-64) populations, prime-age (ages 25-54) populations, and the active population, or labor force. The countries shown are the sixteen largest AEs, ordered by economic size. We also show median values for a larger set of thirty-six AEs and for developments in China, at the bottom of the table.
Level-Setting AE Population and Labor Force Growth
AE Population and Labor Force Growth Since 2014 (percent)
The first column shows wide variation in the growth of working-age populations. Growth has been negative for seven of the countries shown, with particularly marked declines in Japan, Italy, Poland, and Taiwan. Growth has also been negative in the median AE. Yet several countries have seen gains of more than 5 percent. Growth in the U.S. was solidly positive at 3 percent, but not near the top.
Variation in the growth of prime-age populations, shown in the second column, has been still more striking, ranging from dramatic declines (Japan, Germany, Italy, and Spain) to marked increases (Canada, Australia, and Sweden). Again, the U.S. stands toward the higher end of the distribution. Larger declines in the prime-age population than in the working-age population (note the gap in Spain) imply that a large share of the population has moved into the 55-64 age group and will drop out of the traditional working-age population over the coming decade. As we’ll see shortly, the variation in countries’ demographic trajectories is mostly an immigration story.
The third column of the table shows labor force growth since 2014. The contrast with demographic developments is stark. Where working-age populations have grown, active populations have grown more strongly; where working-age populations have declined, active populations have defied demographic gravity. (Indeed, in our broader sample of thirty-six AEs, only Greece and Latvia saw small labor force declines.) In several cases, the contrast can only be termed remarkable. Japan, for example, saw 6 percent labor force growth on a 7 percent drop in its working-age population. Germany saw almost 6 percent growth on a 2 percent decline in its working-age population—and a drop of more than 8 percent in the high-attachment prime-age population.
A Boost from Labor Force Participation
The gap between growth in active and working-age populations implies that labor force participation has been increasing. The table below illustrates this phenomenon across three dimensions, showing changes in participation rates among the traditional working-age population (ages 15-64), working-age women, and the “young old” (ages 65 to 74).
Rising Female and “Young Old” Participation Have Insulated AE Labor Forces
Changes in Labor Force Participation Since 2014 (percentage points)
As shown in the first column, the trend toward increased participation has been essentially universal across AEs. Gains in several countries peaked at 5 percentage points (ppt), with the median country seeing an increase of 4 ppt. Higher participation among women made an important contribution to the general increase, with the median country seeing an increase of more than 5 ppt. title: When Is Monetary Policy Transmission Strongest?
text:
Prior research shows the Federal Reserve responds more aggressively to demand-driven inflation than supply-driven inflation, consistent with its balanced approach when policy goals for employment and prices conflict. While this implies that short-term interest rates are more sensitive to demand-related conditions, recent analysis shows the same holds for longer-horizon yields. Policy surprises primarily pass through to longer-horizon forward rates during demand-driven inflationary episodes. With the recent reemergence of supply-side inflationary pressures, monetary policy surprises are likely to have a smaller impact on longer-horizon yields.
The reemergence of supply-driven inflation pressures since the pandemic has prompted a deeper examination of how the underlying sources of inflation affect monetary policy. Recent evidence indicates that whether inflation is driven by supply or demand is a key determinant of the Federal Reserve’s interest rate policy decisions (Hoffman, Manea, and Mojon 2024 and Kakhbod, Kermani, and Maciel 2026). Specifically, the Fed tends to be more aggressive in responding to demand-driven than supply-driven inflationary pressures. This asymmetry in monetary policy decisions aligns with the Fed’s 2025 Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, which discusses a “balanced approach” when employment and price stability goals conflict, as they tend to do in response to supply shocks.
While this evidence implies that short-term interest rates tend to be more sensitive to demand-driven inflationary pressures, it is not known if the same sensitivity holds true for longer-horizon yields. Financial markets may take into account the underlying reasons behind Fed policy changes, which itself depends on the source of inflationary pressure. In this Economic Letter, we assess whether the degree to which monetary policy surprises are transmitted to bond markets varies with the source of inflationary pressure at the time of the policy change.
To address this question, we use high-frequency data from the San Francisco Fed’s U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD), as developed in Acosta et al. (2026). This data set isolates policy “surprises”—the unexpected component of Fed announcements. Because these surprises are not already anticipated, tracking their immediate impact on forward rates—what the market expects interest rates to be in the future—provides a relatively clean measure of monetary policy transmission. We test whether the pass-through of these surprises into Treasury forward rates is associated with the underlying source of inflation, using the San Francisco Fed’s supply- and demand-driven inflation breakdown. Our analysis indicates that these surprises primarily pass through to longer-horizon forward rates during demand-driven inflationary episodes. That is, monetary policy transmission is strongest during episodes of demand-driven inflationary pressures. This also implies that because supply-side inflation pressures have increased in recent years, monetary policy shocks will likely have a more muted impact on longer-horizon yields.
The source of inflation pressure matters
Our analysis uses the San Franscisco Fed’s Supply- and Demand-Driven PCE Inflation data series which separates personal consumption expenditures inflation into distinct components. The series is based on methodology developed in Shapiro (2026) that identifies these drivers by assessing the joint movement of price and quantity indexes within individual categories. When prices and quantities move in the same direction, the change is attributed to demand-side factors, and when they move in opposite directions, it is attributed to supply-side factors.

title: Should We Be Confident about Consumer Confidence’s Ability to Predict Spending?
text:
Should We Be Confident about Consumer Confidence’s Ability to Predict Spending?
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Conventional wisdom suggests consumers’ willingness to spend on discretionary goods and services is tied to how confident they are about their economic situation. Does this mean measures of consumer confidence can help forecast consumer spending?
- Consumer confidence can help estimate consumer spending, but its predictive power is small. Moreover, adding other explanatory variables reduces the predictive power of consumer confidence.
- Over the past four decades, unemployment has had much greater predictive power than consumer confidence. Specifically, the change in the unemployment rate has had roughly 10 times the effect on real PCE growth that the change in consumer confidence has shown.
- Changes in real disposable personal income and stock prices were also more helpful in predicting consumer spending than consumer confidence was.
Measures of consumer attitudes about the present or future tend to be followed closely by the financial media. Consumer attitudes are monitored closely because conventional wisdom holds that a person’s willingness to spend on discretionary goods and services depends importantly on how confident they are about their personal economic situation. Accordingly, the argument goes, a person is more likely to buy an automobile or splurge on an expensive vacation if they are optimistic about their current or future economic situation than if they are pessimistic about their situation. And since consumer spending comprises roughly two-thirds of final sales to domestic purchasers, the strength or weakness of consumer outlays is a key determinant of the health of the overall economy.
Moreover, because forecasting economic activity is of great importance to firms and policymakers, it seems reasonable to assume that measures of consumer confidence or sentiment can help predict consumer spending. But do they?
One senior Federal Reserve official recently asserted that “the link between sentiment data and consumer spending has been weak. It’s not been a strong link at all.”See then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell’s May 7, 2025, press conference. This statement suggests that some economic policymakers — and perhaps economists — see less value using consumer confidence to predict consumer spending.
Measures of Consumer Attitudes
There are two main measures of consumer attitudes, and both are reported on a monthly basis. The first is the Index of Consumer Sentiment published by the University of Michigan Institute for Social Research, and the second is the Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index.Those interested in the construction of the two indexes are referred to details provided by each organization. See details about the University of Michigan index and details about the Conference Board series (PDF). Moreover, both entities survey consumers’ sentiment/confidence in the present and their expectations in the future. This blog post will focus on consumer attitudes in the present.
The figure below offers some support for the assertion that consumer confidence may not help much to predict consumer spending. The figure plots the average of the consumer sentiment and consumer confidence indexes (hereafter “consumer confidence”) and the 12-month percent change in real personal consumption expenditures (PCE). From 2014 to 2018, consumer confidence rose sharply, nearly reaching the all-time high seen in early 2000. At the same time, the growth of real PCE remained relatively constant. In a similar fashion, consumer confidence has recently plunged to levels last seen in 2012, but — again — the growth of real PCE has remained relatively constant.

title: Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
text:
Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
November 2026
27 November 2026
External communication
Agreement for Sweden to join T2
On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.
Market operations and market infrastructure and payments
Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral
On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.
Macroprudential policy and financial stability
Financial Stability Review – November 2026
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release.
Banknotes and coins
2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study, together with a related press release, are available on the ECB’s website.

title: ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
text:
- PRESS RELEASE
ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
27 November 2026
- median consumer perceptions of inflation over the past 12 months and expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased significantly, while median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased slightly and those for five years ahead were unchanged;
- expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months declined, while expectations for spending growth over the next 12 months were unchanged;
- expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased, while the expected unemployment rate in 12 months’ time decreased;
- expectations for growth in the price of homes over the next 12 months decreased, while expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged.
Inflation
In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).
Income and consumption
Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.
Economic growth and labour market
Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.
Housing and credit access

As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (3.8%) than in the highest income quintile (3.0%). title: The Bank of Japan's Semiannual Report on Currency and Monetary Control
text:
Introduction
The Bank of Japan submits to the Diet its Semiannual Report on Currency and Monetary Control every June and December. I am pleased to have this opportunity today to talk about recent economic and financial developments and about the Bank's conduct of monetary policy.
1. Economic and Financial Developments
I will first explain recent economic and financial developments.
Japan's economy has recovered moderately, although some weakness has been seen in part, partly due to the impact of the situation in the Middle East. Exports have increased moderately, against the backdrop of a solid increase in global AI-related demand. Corporate profits have been at high levels, and business fixed investment has been on a moderate increasing trend, despite being affected by a rise in construction costs. Private consumption has been resilient against the background of an improvement in the employment and income situation, despite the impact of factors such as price increases. With regard to the outlook, Japan's economy is expected to continue growing moderately, albeit at a decelerated rate. This is because, although the rise in energy and raw material prices is expected to push down economic activity, the economy is likely to be underpinned by factors such as the government's various measures and accommodative financial conditions, in addition to an increase in AI-related demand.
On the price front, despite factors such as the effects of the government's measures to reduce the household burden of higher energy prices, the year-on-year rate of increase in the consumer price index (CPI) for all items excluding fresh food has been rising moderately, being at around 2 percent recently, as the effects of a rise in import prices have been emerging, with moves to pass on wage increases to selling prices continuing. Regarding the outlook, the rate of increase is likely to accelerate to a level clearly above 2 percent. This is because, with moves to pass on wage increases to selling prices continuing, the rise in crude oil prices is expected to push up prices, mainly of energy and goods, and the rise in the prices of semiconductors and other items, reflecting the increase in global AI-related demand, and the depreciation of the yen thus far are likely to lead to an increase in prices, mainly of durable goods. Meanwhile, with a sense of labor shortage continuing to be strong, the mechanism in which wages and prices rise moderately in interaction with each other has been operating, and medium- to long-term inflation expectations are at around 2 percent. In this situation, underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of 2 percent.
There are various risks to the outlook for economic activity and prices. It is necessary to continue to pay attention to the impact of factors such as the situation in the Middle East, the expansion in AI-related demand, and developments in foreign exchange rates. Given that firms' behavior has been shifting more toward raising wages and prices and there are various factors that could drive up prices, there is a risk that medium- to long-term inflation expectations will rise and underlying CPI inflation will deviate upward to a level above the price stability target of 2 percent. Meanwhile, Japan's financial system has maintained stability on the whole. The Bank judges that, even in the case of an adjustment in the real economy at home and abroad and in global financial markets, the financial system is likely to remain highly robust on the whole, mainly because Japanese financial institutions have sufficient capital bases.
2. Conduct of Monetary Policy
Next, I will explain the Bank's conduct of monetary policy.

title: Considerations at the intersection of payments and tokenized markets
text:
Thank you for inviting me to return and speak today.1 I am delighted to be here during a transformational time in payments. Two years ago, I spoke at The Clearing House's annual conference, where I discussed the roles that the private sector and the Federal Reserve play in payments.2 I argued that the public and private sectors have distinct but complementary roles. In particular, I emphasized that the private sector, through competition, is best positioned to develop solutions that benefit businesses and consumers and to fulfill a clear market need.
The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate, assessing potential risks to financial stability, and regularly engaging with the industry to better understand market challenges. Related to this last role, it's important to note that my remarks today are informed by rich, ongoing discussions I conduct with industry participants across a variety of forums, including a recent payments innovation roundtable I hosted at the Federal Reserve with participants from across traditional and decentralized finance, or DeFi.3
Turning to the timely themes of the conference, many of the sessions focused on the evolving payments landscape, including the state of competition, technological advancements, and readiness for the future. With this backdrop in mind, today I will discuss some considerations for tokenization in the payment system with an eye toward the future and, in particular, the intersection of this technological advancement with existing systems and markets. To be clear, in this context, my focus is on the concept that a financial instrument can be represented digitally in "token" form and transacted on a new platform or technology, such as a distributed ledger technology like blockchain.4
Although the terms "blockchain," "tokenization," and "smart contract" are widely used, to ensure we are on the same page, I want to give a simple explanation of each of these concepts. A blockchain is simply a database that can have a variety of management properties, such as who can hold a copy of the database, who can read the database, who can change the database, and how the database can be updated. The word block means data are added to the existing database in "blocks"—much like adding a new sheet of data to an existing Excel file.5
Tokenization refers to the process of altering the properties of one form of an asset so that it can be transferred and used on a different platform than its current one. For example, if you go to a casino, you cannot use physical currency at the tables or machines. But you can take your cash and buy poker chips to use on the tables. In this world, poker chips are a tokenized version of physical cash that can be used instead of cash.
Finally, a smart contract is simply a piece of code that is embedded in the database and can be triggered to execute an action at a given point of time or under a particular set of conditions. The key aspect of a smart contract is that all conditions of the code must be met simultaneously for the action to occur and be recorded on the blockchain. Smart contracts allow financial trades to be programmable, which is appealing for automating trades.
In any financial trades on a blockchain, there is an object being bought (say, a tokenized share of stock) and there is a tokenized payment instrument being used to settle the trade. For example, stablecoins are starting to be used behind the scenes to settle obligations among participants in card networks. And The Clearing House is one of several groups building a network for clearing and settling tokenized deposits, which are digital transformations of the digits in your checking account that can then be used as a payment instrument to execute a blockchain trade.
